questions.stem: Grevillea Grocers buys a coffee machine for $12,000, pays $300 for delivery and $700 for installation, and takes out a first-year maintenance contract for $500 (all excluding GST). At what cost is the machine recorded?
questions.explanation: The cost of a non-current asset includes every cost needed to get it ready for use, so delivery and installation are added: $12,000 + $300 + $700 = $13,000. The maintenance contract is an ongoing running cost of using the machine, so it is an expense.

questions.stem: Grevillea Grocers buys a delivery van for $44,000 including GST, paying cash. Which entry records the purchase?
options: Dr Vehicle 40,000; Cr GST Clearing 4,000; Cr Bank 36,000
Dr Vehicle Expense 40,000; Dr GST Clearing 4,000; Cr Bank 44,000
Dr Vehicle 40,000; Dr GST Clearing 4,000; Cr Bank 44,000
Dr Vehicle 44,000; Cr Bank 44,000
questions.explanation: The van is a non-current asset recorded at its cost excluding GST, and the $4,000 GST paid is debited to GST Clearing because it can be claimed back. It is not an expense, because it will provide benefits over several years.

questions.stem: Grevillea Grocers buys refrigeration equipment for $33,000 including GST. It pays a deposit of $8,000 and finances the rest with a loan from its bank. Which entry records the purchase?
options: Dr Equipment 30,000; Dr GST Clearing 3,000; Cr Loan 33,000
Dr Equipment 25,000; Dr GST Clearing 3,000; Cr Bank 8,000; Cr Loan 20,000
Dr Equipment 30,000; Dr GST Clearing 3,000; Cr Bank 8,000; Cr Loan 25,000
Dr Equipment 33,000; Cr Bank 8,000; Cr Loan 25,000
questions.explanation: The equipment is recorded at its full cost excluding GST and the GST is claimed in full, however the purchase is financed; Bank falls by the deposit and the loan covers the remaining $25,000. Recording only the financed part as the asset's cost understates the equipment.

questions.stem: How does buying equipment financed by a long-term loan affect Grevillea Grocers' debt ratio?
options: It decreases the debt ratio, because the loan is non-current rather than current.
It increases the debt ratio, because liabilities and assets rise by the same amount.
It decreases the debt ratio, because total assets rise when the equipment is added.
It leaves the debt ratio unchanged, because assets and liabilities both increase.
questions.explanation: Adding the same amount to liabilities and assets raises the proportion of assets financed by debt whenever the ratio is below 100%, so the debt ratio rises and stability weakens. Equal increases leave the difference unchanged but not the ratio.

questions.stem: Each monthly loan repayment on the refrigeration equipment includes principal and interest. How is it recorded?
options: the interest reduces the Loan liability and the principal is an expense
the principal reduces the Loan liability and the interest is an expense
the whole repayment is an expense in the Income Statement
the whole repayment reduces the Loan liability
questions.explanation: Repaying principal settles part of the obligation, so it reduces the liability, while interest is the cost of borrowing for the period and is an expense. Treating the whole repayment as an expense would understate profit and overstate the loan.

questions.stem: Depreciation of a non-current asset is best described as:
options: allocating the asset's cost, less its residual value, as an expense over its useful life
reducing the asset to its current market value at the end of every reporting period
setting aside cash each year so that the business can afford to replace the asset
recording the cash paid for repairs and maintenance on the asset during the period
questions.explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset over the periods that benefit from it, applying the accrual basis. It does not set aside any cash and is not a valuation, so the carrying value will usually differ from market value.

questions.stem: The coffee machine cost $13,000, has a residual value of $1,000 and a useful life of four years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
questions.explanation: Straight-line depreciation is (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life = ($13,000 − $1,000) ÷ 4 = $3,000. Ignoring the residual value gives $3,250, which would depreciate the machine below what it is expected to be worth at the end.

questions.stem: Grevillea Grocers buys shelving for $18,000 on 1 October and depreciates it at $6,000 a year using the straight-line method. What depreciation is recorded for the year ended 30 June?
questions.explanation: The shelving was used for nine months of the reporting period, so 9/12 × $6,000 = $4,500. Recording a full year's $6,000 charges an expense for three months before the asset was owned.

questions.stem: Which General Journal entry records depreciation of the delivery van?
options: Dr Depreciation of Vehicle; Cr Vehicle
Dr Depreciation of Vehicle; Cr Accumulated Depreciation of Vehicle
Dr Accumulated Depreciation of Vehicle; Cr Depreciation of Vehicle
Dr Depreciation of Vehicle; Cr Bank
questions.explanation: Depreciation is an expense, debited, and the credit goes to Accumulated Depreciation, a negative asset that builds up over the van's life while the Vehicle account stays at cost. No cash is paid, so Bank is not affected.

questions.stem: The carrying value of a non-current asset is:
options: its current market value
its cost plus accumulated depreciation
its cost less accumulated depreciation
its cost less this year's depreciation
questions.explanation: Carrying value is what the asset is reported at in the Balance Sheet: cost less all the depreciation recorded to date. Deducting only this year's depreciation ignores the depreciation of earlier years.

questions.stem: Under the reducing balance method, each year's depreciation is calculated as:
options: the difference between the asset's cost and its current market value
a fixed percentage of the asset's carrying value at the start of the year
a fixed percentage of the asset's original cost in every year of its life
the cost less residual value, divided equally over the useful life
questions.explanation: Reducing balance applies the same rate to a carrying value that shrinks each year, so the expense falls over time. A fixed percentage of the original cost gives the same amount every year, which is the straight-line method.

questions.stem: Grevillea Grocers' delivery van cost $40,000 and is depreciated at 25% a year using the reducing balance method. What is its carrying value at the end of the second year?
questions.explanation: Year 1 depreciation is 25% × $40,000 = $10,000, leaving $30,000; year 2 is 25% × $30,000 = $7,500, leaving $22,500. Charging 25% of the original cost each year gives $20,000, which is the straight-line result.

questions.stem: A computer cost $8,000 and is depreciated at 40% a year using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation expense in the third year?
questions.explanation: Year 1: 40% × $8,000 = $3,200, leaving $4,800. Year 2: 40% × $4,800 = $1,920, leaving $2,880. Year 3: 40% × $2,880 = $1,152. The figure of $1,920 is the second year's charge, and $1,728 is the carrying value at the end of year 3.

questions.stem: Compared with the straight-line method, the reducing balance method in the first year of an asset's life gives:
options: higher depreciation, lower net profit and a higher carrying value
the same depreciation, but a lower carrying value in the Balance Sheet
higher depreciation, lower net profit and a lower carrying value
lower depreciation, higher net profit and a higher carrying value
questions.explanation: Reducing balance charges most depreciation early, so the first year's expense is higher, profit lower and the asset's carrying value lower. In later years the pattern reverses as the reducing balance charge falls below the straight-line charge.

questions.stem: Which asset would most suitably be depreciated using the reducing balance method?
options: shop shelving that provides the same benefit every year for ten years
a building whose benefit to the business is spread evenly over decades
a counter that is used in exactly the same way each year it is owned
a laptop that loses most of its usefulness in its first two years
questions.explanation: Reducing balance matches a larger expense to the early years, which faithfully represents an asset whose benefits are greatest when new, such as computer equipment. Assets that give even benefits over their lives suit the straight-line method.

questions.stem: How does the choice of depreciation method affect the Cash Flow Statement?
options: Straight-line gives higher cash outflows in the later years of the asset.
The method changes the cash paid to buy the asset in the first year.
It does not change cash flows, because depreciation involves no cash.
Reducing balance gives higher cash outflows in the early years of the asset.
questions.explanation: Depreciation allocates a cost already paid, so neither method moves any cash and the Cash Flow Statement is identical. The method affects only the Income Statement expense and the Balance Sheet carrying value.

questions.stem: Over the whole useful life of an asset, if both methods depreciate it to the same residual value, how do straight-line and reducing balance compare?
options: Total depreciation differs, because each method has a different cost.
Total depreciation is the same; only its timing across the years differs.
Reducing balance gives a larger total, because each year's rate is higher.
Straight-line gives a larger total, because it ignores the carrying value.
questions.explanation: Either way the total expense is cost less residual value; the methods only spread it differently, with reducing balance front-loading the expense. The cost of the asset is the same whichever method is chosen.

questions.stem: The owner of Grevillea Grocers wants to switch from reducing balance to straight-line depreciation this year only because it will make profit look higher before she sells the business. What is the main concern?
options: It is not allowed, because a method once chosen can never be changed for any reason.
It understates profit, which would reduce the price the owner receives for the business.
It reduces comparability and is chosen to mislead a buyer rather than to reflect the asset's use.
It breaches the going concern assumption, because the business is about to be sold.
questions.explanation: A change in method makes this year's report harder to compare with earlier years, and making it to inflate profit for a sale is biased and unethical. A method can be changed if it better reflects the pattern of use, but not to mislead a buyer.

questions.stem: Increasing the estimated useful life of the delivery van from five to eight years, with no other change, would:
options: increase the cash available, because less depreciation is paid
decrease the annual depreciation and increase net profit
increase the annual depreciation and decrease net profit
decrease the annual depreciation and decrease the carrying value
questions.explanation: Spreading the same depreciable amount over more years lowers each year's charge, raising profit and the carrying value. Depreciation is not paid in cash, so cash is unaffected.

questions.stem: Before recording the disposal of a non-current asset part way through the year, the business must first:
options: record a full year of depreciation on the asset for the current period
write the asset down to its market value at the date of disposal
reverse all the depreciation recorded on the asset in earlier years
record depreciation from the start of the year up to the date of disposal
questions.explanation: Depreciation must be brought up to date so that the carrying value at the date of sale is correct and the asset's use this year is expensed. A full year's charge would include months after the asset was gone.

questions.stem: Equipment that cost $20,000 has accumulated depreciation of $14,000. It is sold for $7,700 cash including GST. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
options: loss of $12,300
loss of $6,000
profit of $1,000
profit of $1,700
questions.explanation: GST applies to a cash disposal, so the proceeds are $7,000, and against a carrying value of $6,000 that is a profit of $1,000. Using the GST-inclusive $7,700 overstates the profit by the $700 owed to the ATO.

questions.stem: When the equipment is sold for $7,700 cash including GST, how is GST Clearing affected?
options: credited $700
debited $700
credited $770
not affected, as GST does not apply to disposals
questions.explanation: The study design applies GST to the cash disposal of a non-current asset, so $700 is credited to GST Clearing as GST collected. GST is left out only when the asset is disposed of by trade-in.

questions.stem: A display freezer cost $15,000 and is depreciated at $2,400 a year straight-line. Accumulated depreciation was $7,200 at 1 July. It is sold for $4,400 cash including GST on 31 December. What is the loss on disposal?
questions.explanation: Six months' depreciation of $1,200 brings accumulated depreciation to $8,400 and the carrying value to $6,600; proceeds excluding GST are $4,000, so the loss is $2,600. Forgetting the extra six months of depreciation gives a loss of $3,800.

questions.stem: How is a profit on the disposal of a non-current asset reported?
options: as part of net sales in the Income Statement
as an increase in capital in the Balance Sheet
as an operating inflow in the Cash Flow Statement
as other revenue in the Income Statement
questions.explanation: A profit on disposal increases owner's equity through the business's activities, so it is revenue, but it is not from selling inventory, so it is other revenue rather than sales. The cash received is an investing inflow, not operating.

questions.stem: Under the study design, how is GST treated when a non-current asset is disposed of by trade-in?
options: GST is charged on the original cost of the old asset.
GST does not apply to the trade-in disposal of the old asset.
GST is charged on the trade-in value of the old asset.
GST is charged on the carrying value of the old asset.
questions.explanation: The study design states that GST will not apply where an asset is disposed of by trade-in, so the trade-in value is the proceeds in full. GST does apply when an asset is sold for cash.

questions.stem: Grevillea Grocers trades in its old van (cost $35,000, accumulated depreciation $24,000) for $9,000 on a new van costing $55,000 plus GST of $5,500. What is the loss on disposal and the cash paid?
options: Loss of $2,000; cash paid $51,500
Loss of $2,000; cash paid $46,000
Profit of $2,000; cash paid $51,500
Loss of $11,000; cash paid $60,500
questions.explanation: The old van's carrying value is $11,000 and the trade-in, which carries no GST, is $9,000, so the loss is $2,000. The new van costs $60,500 including GST, and the trade-in covers $9,000, leaving $51,500 to pay. Leaving out the GST on the new van gives $46,000.

questions.stem: In the Cash Flow Statement, the cash received from selling an old vehicle is reported as:
options: other revenue
an investing inflow
an operating inflow
a financing inflow
questions.explanation: The purchase and sale of non-current assets are investing activities, so the proceeds are an investing inflow. Other revenue is an Income Statement item, and only the profit on disposal, not the full proceeds, appears there.

questions.stem: On the trade-in, how much of the old van's $9,000 trade-in value appears in the Cash Flow Statement?
options: $9,000, as a financing inflow from the dealer
$2,000, as an operating outflow for the loss
none, because no cash is received for the trade-in
$9,000, as an investing inflow from the sale
questions.explanation: A trade-in reduces the amount paid for the new asset rather than bringing in cash, so only the $51,500 actually paid appears, as an investing outflow. The loss on disposal is a non-cash expense and does not appear in the Cash Flow Statement.

questions.stem: What is the effect of recording a loss on disposal of a non-current asset?
options: Net profit increases, because the asset is removed from the Balance Sheet.
Net profit decreases, with no change to cash at the time the loss is recognised.
Net profit decreases, and cash decreases by the amount of the loss.
Net profit is unaffected, because the loss reduces capital directly.
questions.explanation: A loss on disposal is an expense, so it reduces profit, but it is the gap between carrying value and proceeds rather than a payment of cash. The cash effect is the proceeds received, which is an inflow, not an outflow.

questions.stem: Grevillea Grocers sold equipment for cash at a profit of $1,000 but forgot to bring depreciation of $800 up to the date of sale. What is the effect on its net profit for the year?
options: Net profit is understated by $800, because the profit on disposal is understated by that amount.
Net profit is overstated by $1,600, because depreciation and the disposal profit are both wrong.
Net profit is correct overall, but depreciation and the profit on disposal are both understated by $800.
Net profit is overstated by $800, because depreciation is understated and the disposal profit is correct.
questions.explanation: Missing $800 of depreciation leaves the carrying value $800 too high, so the true profit on disposal is $1,800, not $1,000. The $800 understatement of disposal profit exactly offsets the $800 understatement of depreciation expense, so net profit is unchanged, but both items are misclassified.

questions.stem: In the Balance Sheet, the delivery van (cost $40,000, accumulated depreciation $17,500) is reported as:
options: a non-current asset at its expected resale value at the end of its life
a non-current asset at cost less accumulated depreciation, $22,500
a non-current asset at cost, $40,000, with depreciation shown as a liability
a current asset at carrying value, $22,500, because it is used every day
questions.explanation: Non-current assets are shown at cost with accumulated depreciation deducted, giving the carrying value of $22,500. Accumulated depreciation is a negative asset, not a liability, because nothing is owed to anyone.

questions.stem: Depreciation expense is recorded each year even though no cash is paid. Which accounting assumption requires this?
options: the entity assumption, because the asset belongs to the business, not the owner
the going concern assumption, because the asset will be sold at the end of its life
the period assumption alone, because cash must be measured in each period
the accrual basis assumption, because the asset's benefits are consumed in that period
questions.explanation: Expenses are recognised when the consumption of goods and services can be measured, so the part of the asset used up each period is expensed then, whether or not cash moves. Going concern assumes the business continues, not that the asset will be sold.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes depreciation from repairs to a non-current asset?
options: Depreciation allocates the asset's cost; repairs are a separate expense paid in cash when incurred.
Depreciation is paid in cash each year; repairs are added to the asset's cost to increase its value.
Depreciation is recorded only when the asset is sold; repairs are recorded every period.
Depreciation is a liability for future replacement; repairs are a reduction in capital.
questions.explanation: Depreciation spreads the original cost over the useful life without any cash, while routine repairs are a separate expense for the period in which they are incurred. Adding routine repairs to the asset's cost would overstate the asset and profit.

questions.stem: Grevillea Grocers decides to dispose of its old refrigeration units by paying a licensed recycler rather than sending them to landfill for free. Which consideration does this decision reflect most directly?
options: an environmental consideration, accepting a higher cost to reduce harm
a financial consideration only, because the recycler is cheaper than landfill
the going concern assumption, because the business will need new units
the comparability characteristic, because other grocers recycle as well
questions.explanation: Paying more to dispose of refrigerants and metals safely reduces environmental harm at a financial cost, which is the kind of ethical trade-off owners must weigh. It is not the cheaper option, so it is not a purely financial decision.

questions.stem: Which cost should be expensed in the year incurred rather than added to the cost of a new delivery van?
options: fuel used by the van in its first month
the purchase price of the van
fitting shelving inside the van before it is first used
delivery of the van to the business
questions.explanation: Fuel is a running cost of using the van, so it is an expense of the period. Costs that get the van ready for use, such as delivery and fitting out its shelving, are part of its cost.

questions.stem: Two identical businesses buy identical $30,000 vans with no residual value. One uses straight-line over five years; the other reducing balance at 40%. Which statement is correct for the first year?
options: The straight-line business reports $6,000 more depreciation and $6,000 less profit.
The reducing balance business reports $6,000 less cash than the other business.
Both businesses report the same profit, because their vans cost the same amount.
The reducing balance business reports $6,000 more depreciation and $6,000 less profit.
questions.explanation: Straight-line gives $30,000 ÷ 5 = $6,000 and reducing balance gives 40% × $30,000 = $12,000, so the reducing balance business reports $6,000 more expense and $6,000 less profit. Cash is the same for both, because depreciation involves no payment.

questions.stem: Which indicator is affected when Grevillea Grocers records a year's depreciation on its equipment?
options: working capital ratio, because current assets fall
quick assets ratio, because prepayments rise
cash flow cover, because operating cash falls
return on assets, because both net profit and total assets fall
questions.explanation: Depreciation reduces net profit and the carrying value of non-current assets, so return on assets changes. It does not affect current assets, current liabilities or any cash flow, so the liquidity indicators and cash flow cover are unchanged.

questions.stem: The residual value of a non-current asset is:
options: the amount the business expects to receive for the asset at the end of its useful life
the carrying value of the asset at the end of the current reporting period
the total depreciation the asset is expected to incur over its useful life
the amount still owing on any loan used to finance the asset's purchase
questions.explanation: Residual value is the estimated amount the asset will be worth to the business when it is disposed of at the end of its useful life, and it is not depreciated. The carrying value changes every period as depreciation accumulates.

questions.stem: Accumulated Depreciation of Equipment is classified as:
options: a negative non-current asset, deducted from Equipment
a non-current liability for replacing the equipment
an expense in the Income Statement each period
a reduction in owner's equity in the Balance Sheet
questions.explanation: Accumulated depreciation is the total depreciation recorded to date and is deducted from the asset's cost to give its carrying value. The expense for the period is the separate Depreciation account, which appears in the Income Statement.
